Synthesizing the data across both tracks does not reveal a consistent ordinal ranking, and we do not claim one: the same three models (GPT-5, Opus, Sonnet) occupy the top group in both tracks, but their internal order permutes (GPT-5 leads Track A, Opus leads Track B), and Track B additionally places four of the seven models in an outright tie at 0/8 objectives met, a degeneracy Track A's continuous score never produces. What does hold is a coarser claim: the same three models separate from the same other four in both tracks, and the gap between that top group and the rest widens sharply in agentic repair --- a large effect that survives the reordering even though the exact ranking does not. This divergence supports a secondary objective of the reference suite: to differentiate between models that merely emit syntactically simulatable RTL --- a baseline capability shared by most evaluated models --- and those capable of producing, or iteratively refining, silicon to a standard acceptable to a competent hardware engineer.

\section{Limitations and Threats to Validity}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Audit scope.} The external audit (Sections~\ref{sec:audit-method}--\ref{sec:audit-results}) covers all 50 public designs of RTLLM v2.0 (46 audited, 4 reported \texttt{unsupported} with a stated reason each) and reports a structural finding, rather than a measurement, for CVDP given its withheld reference solutions. It does not cover every RTL-generation benchmark in current use. In particular, VerilogEval~\cite{liu2023verilogeval,pinckney2024revisiting} --- arguably the field's most-cited benchmark --- is not audited here; this is a scope decision made to keep the first application of this methodology focused on one primary target (RTLLM v2.0) and one structural finding (CVDP) rather than a principled exclusion, and we name it explicitly rather than let the omission pass silently. ChipBench, ArchXBench, SLDB, ProtocolLLM, ChipVerilog, and RTL-BenchLS are likewise out of scope for this round. Coverage of the Si2 LLM Benchmarking Coalition's evolving CVDP-derived leaderboard is necessarily a snapshot rather than a standing measurement. The audit measures testbench sensitivity to a fixed, generic operator set; a testbench could in principle be robust to our specific operators while remaining weak against fault classes we do not inject. The methodology and tooling are open specifically so others can extend the operator set or apply it to additional benchmarks. The build-convention normalization described in Section~\ref{sec:audit-method} is bounded strictly to what a target's own documented build recipe already specifies (e.g., a per-design makefile's stated candidate-module contract); it is not a search over renamings intended to maximize the reported compatibility count, and every applied alias is recorded per design so a third party can audit the boundary between ``ran as vendor-intended'' and ``ran after our own compatibility work'' for themselves. More broadly, ``rigor'' as measured here is specifically testbench sensitivity to injected mutants; it is not a claim about a benchmark's specification correctness, golden-reference correctness, task representativeness, contamination resistance, or scoring methodology, none of which this audit examines.

\paragraph{Repository visibility.} As of this writing, the GitHub repository is private. It is Apache-2.0 licensed and structured for public release, gated on a maintainer-run pre-publication checklist (history scrub, image publication by digest, this paper's submission) rather than on any remaining technical work; every claim in this paper of the form ``published,'' ``open,'' or ``publicly available'' describes that intended end state, not current public accessibility. We call this out explicitly rather than let a reader assume public availability at submission time.

\paragraph{Sensitivity is not the same as correctness.} A high kill rate establishes that a testbench is sensitive to the specific faults injected; it does not establish that the testbench's own oracle (the golden reference and the pass/fail check itself) is correct, nor that a testbench with a high kill rate would correctly accept every valid alternative implementation (specificity, or false-rejection rate, in the terminology of software mutation testing). RTLLM's \texttt{radix2\_div} illustrates the first point directly, and does so before mutation even begins: its unmodified golden reference already fails its own testbench, so the design never clears baseline validation and no mutant is ever injected into it (it is reported \texttt{unsupported}, with zero mutants generated). A testbench whose own reference fails it cannot be assigned a meaningful kill rate at all, which is a sharper version of the same point --- sensitivity is undefined when the oracle is already wrong. We do not attempt to measure false-rejection rate in this work, since it would require independently correct alternative implementations or a formal specification per design, neither of which is available for RTLLM's designs; this is future work, not a property this audit currently reports.

\paragraph{Mutant generation, equivalence, and the role of the seed.} GateTruth's generator deterministically enumerates every syntactically viable mutation site for its fixed generic operator set; no sampling of mutants occurs, so the fixed seed governs only execution order (relevant to how simulation timeouts interact with per-run budgets under sequential execution, Section~\ref{sec:rigor}), not which or how many mutants are generated. We do not detect or exclude equivalent mutants (mutants that are syntactically distinct but behaviorally identical to the original under the design's reachable state space); any equivalent mutants present would depress the reported kill rate relative to a hypothetical equivalent-mutant-free count, so our reported rates are, if anything, a conservative (lower) estimate of true fault-detection sensitivity. Mutant counts per RTLLM design range from 1 to 115 (median 10.5); we report every design's raw count rather than filtering by a minimum, but results built on very small counts (as low as 1) carry correspondingly less statistical weight, and we flag this explicitly rather than let a headline percentage stand without its denominator (Section~\ref{sec:audit-results}). We also do not perform a manual audit distinguishing genuine functional-mismatch kills from incidental simulator artifacts (e.g., uninitialized-signal propagation), nor a manual audit reclassifying survivors; verdicts throughout are produced by the automated compile/simulate/pass-string pipeline described in Section~\ref{sec:audit-method}. Finally, RTLLM's 46 audited designs share common benchmark authorship, testbench-writing conventions, and a single vendor's coding style; they should not be treated as fully independent samples when interpreting the aggregate 74.0\% median or the 72\% below-floor rate.

\paragraph{Pre-layout physical estimates, not signoff values.} The physical metrics reported by GateTruth's own reference suite represent synthesis and static-timing estimates rather than post-place-and-route signoff values. The evaluation flow synthesizes designs utilizing the sky130hd standard-cell library and performs timing analysis via OpenSTA at a single typical-typical process corner. Because the pipeline does not execute placement, routing, or parasitic extraction, the reported area corresponds strictly to pre-layout cell area, and the reported timing reflects pre-layout slack. While a complete place-and-route trajectory was scoped and evaluated during development, it was deferred for the v1.0 release; an open-source routed-flow feasibility assessment failed to meet the requisite reliability thresholds necessary to enforce routed metrics as a scored gate (as documented in the project's decision log). Consequently, the manuscript reports pre-route estimates --- explicitly labeled as such --- and designates a fully routed evaluation track as future work rather than presenting it as a silent approximation. Therefore, PPA comparisons within this paper are rigorously valid within the confines of the pinned evaluation flow, but they must not be extrapolated as predictive of taped-out physical silicon.

\paragraph{Contamination resistance and the bounds of the correctness gate.} Two additional methodological limitations bound the reference suite's claims regarding data contamination and functional correctness. First, the contamination defense operates as a multi-layered deterrent framework --- comprising original-prose specifications, per-task canaries, and hidden test vectors excluded from the public repository. This architecture significantly elevates the computational and operational cost of leaderboard manipulation without theoretically eliminating it; a sophisticated actor capable of reconstructing hidden behavior exclusively from the public smoke testbench is not provably thwarted. A more robust asymmetric-split architecture, incorporating published hash commitments and inference-time specification mutation, is deferred to subsequent iterations. Second, the functional correctness gate is intrinsically bounded by the rigor of its underlying testbenches. We mitigate this limitation --- for our own suite, exactly as we do for the external benchmarks we audit --- by enforcing a $\ge$95\% mutation-kill floor validated under sequential execution (Section~\ref{sec:rigor}). However, mutation testing inherently quantifies a testbench's sensitivity to artificially injected faults, not its completeness against all conceivable real-world defects; notably, only 46 of our own suite's 60 testbenches currently clear this threshold at all (Section~\ref{sec:rigor} reports the 14 that do not, and the two successive corrections --- an unsound equivalence-exclusion mechanism, then a metric that had been silently blending lint and formal kills into what should have been a simulation-only rate --- that moved this figure from a false 60 of 60 down to 46 of 60), and of the 46 that clear it, 2 do so while retaining a small, documented single survivor above the 95\% floor rather than achieving a perfect kill rate. Finally, the reference suite is methodologically constrained: it utilizes English-prose specifications, operates within a single-clock paradigm (wherein clock-domain crossing is modeled structurally rather than via true multi-clock metastability simulation), and is strictly scoped to the previously defined task classes. Three further limitations bound how much weight the PPA denominator and the correctness gate can individually bear. The maintainer-approved reference implementation for each task is a single implementation, AI-drafted and maintainer-reviewed rather than independently authored from scratch (Section~\ref{sec:disclosure}); we have neither a second independent implementation nor a measurement of inter-author variance, so the PPA ratio's denominator carries whatever idiosyncrasy that single drafting-and-review process introduces, and we do not claim it represents an optimal or averaged baseline of any kind. Separately, mutation-kill certification (Section~\ref{sec:rigor}) measures the simulation testbench only; for the 46 of 60 Track A tasks that additionally define formal properties, we do not measure the rigor of those properties themselves (e.g., via vacuity checking or coverage of the property set), and the bounded-model-checking depth used by SymbiYosys is not stated in this paper, so ``formal verification status'' as reported is not independently reproducible from the paper alone, only from the pinned pipeline. Finally, each leaderboard entry is a single sample (pass@1 at $k=1$, temperature zero or provider default); standard practice for LLM code-generation evaluation is typically $n > k$ repeated samples, and Appendix~\ref{app:variance} exists precisely because a single sample is a noisy estimator, particularly for the correctness-gate-dominated Track A score that underlies 96\% or more of most models' composite signal.

\paragraph{Failure-stage taxonomy.} Table~\ref{tab:tracka} reports a score per model but not where failing submissions fail; Appendix~\ref{app:taxonomy} (Table~\ref{tab:taxonomy}) gives the full per-model breakdown, generated from the signed per-sample manifests so it cannot drift from the underlying evidence. Across the reported campaign's 185 failing (model, task) pairs, 17 (9.2\%) never reached a scored submission at all, and we split this bucket into two categories that mean different things rather than merge them into one, as an earlier draft of this paper did. Fourteen (3.3\% of all 420 pairs) failed at the API layer itself --- a dropped TLS connection, a non-2xx HTTP status, or a malformed response body --- before any model output existed to inspect; our harness records these as zero-scored failures without retrying the call, which is a gap in the harness's robustness, not a signal about model capability, and we name it as a limitation rather than silently fold it into a benchmark finding. The remaining 3 pairs did receive a response, but none extracted into a single valid module: all three are Gemini~2.5~Pro submissions truncated at exactly 16{,}380 of the 16{,}384-token cap, i.e. generation ran out of budget mid-declaration. Of the remaining 168 pairs that did produce a scored submission, 78.6\% fail at Stage~0 (lint), 19.6\% at Stage~1 (simulation), and 1.8\% at Stage~2 (formal). Two consequences deserve to be stated plainly rather than left implicit. First, the formal gate discriminates almost nothing: it is the earliest failing stage for 3 of 185 failures campaign-wide, so for practical purposes the correctness verdict is decided by lint and simulation, and the bounded-model-checking layer --- applied to 46 of 60 tasks --- separates essentially no submissions in this campaign. Second, Stages~3--5 (synthesis, static timing, power) are the earliest failing stage for exactly zero submissions: no design that cleared correctness subsequently failed synthesis or timing analysis, so the physical stages act as measurement rather than as a gate. We report both non-binding controls explicitly rather than presenting them as active safeguards.

\paragraph{The lint gate is doing more work than intended.} Inspecting the Stage-0 lint logs directly, 99 of the 132 lint failures (75.0\%, and 58.9\% of all submissions that failed any gate) contain no hard syntax or semantic error: Verilator's default policy escalates certain warning classes --- predominantly implicit bit-width truncation and expansion, \texttt{WIDTHTRUNC} and \texttt{WIDTHEXPAND} --- to a fatal exit, and our lint invocation (\texttt{verilator -{}-lint-only -{}-sv}, Verilator 5.051, \texttt{rev v5.050-40-g6c20fdb7b}) applies no waivers. The per-model split of these width-only failures is uneven: Llama 4 Maverick 19, Haiku 19, Opus 15, GPT-5-mini 14, Sonnet 13, Gemini 2.5 Pro 11, GPT-5 8. We take the defensible position that lint-clean RTL is a legitimate deliverable standard --- implicit width mismatches are a real and commonly-mandated defect class in industry sign-off flows, and Verilator flags them for that reason --- and therefore do not waive them. But we will not have it both ways: because this single gate accounts for roughly half of all zero scores in the campaign (99 of 185) and its firing rate varies 2.4-fold across models (19 for Llama 4 Maverick and Haiku against 8 for GPT-5), Table~\ref{tab:tracka}'s ranking is materially a joint ranking of RTL correctness \emph{and} width-declaration hygiene, and we do not claim it isolates the former. We have not re-simulated the width-only failures with the warning waived, so we cannot report how many would have passed Stage~1; that measurement, and a dual strict/waived leaderboard, are the correct way to settle what share of the ranking each factor contributes, and both are future work rather than results we can claim here. Note also that the escalate-to-fatal behavior is a version-dependent tool default, which is why the exact Verilator revision is pinned above.

\paragraph{What the output-token budget experiment does and does not establish.} Section~\ref{sec:results} and Table~\ref{tab:budget} report both conditions; three caveats bound what they license. First, each condition is a single sample per model, so a per-model delta of a few points is not separable from run-to-run noise --- only two movements are unambiguously established against any plausible noise floor --- GPT-5's $+17.19$ and Gemini's $+13.23$, both far larger than the frontier Anthropic models' measured standard deviations (Appendix~\ref{app:variance}: $\sigma \approx 1.85$--$2.53$) --- and only those two do we treat as established. The remaining movements are smaller than or comparable to that floor and we do not interpret any of them, in either direction: GPT-5-mini's $+1.79$ has no variance estimate to weigh it against (GPT-5-mini was not part of the repeated-run study), and Sonnet's $-2.94$ --- the one model here with a direct estimate --- is slightly above its own measured $\sigma \approx 2.53$, the closest call of the four, which we still treat as within noise rather than as evidence of an effect. Second, the two conditions differ in one respect besides the cap: the 16{,}384-token runs used the hardened response parser described below, while the 4096 runs predate it. That parser change is score-neutral by construction (an unterminated response scored zero under both the old and new code paths, for different reasons), so the score comparison remains attributable to the budget alone; what it does change is the \emph{classification} of some failures, which is why Gemini's no-extraction count rises even as its score rises. Third, we did not sweep intermediate budgets, so we cannot say where the effect saturates: 16{,}384 is sufficient to drive GPT-5's and GPT-5-mini's no-extraction counts to zero, but we have not established it is sufficient for every model on every task, and a still-higher cap might move the ranking again. The claim we defend is narrow and, we think, important: a shared output cap is not a neutral implementation detail, it interacts with how much of its budget a model spends on reasoning, and a benchmark that does not report its cap has not reported its experimental condition.

\paragraph{An extraction defect we found, fixed, and confirmed does \emph{not} explain the above.} While assembling the taxonomy we found a real bug in our own response parser (\texttt{extract\_module\_source}): it stripped a Markdown code fence only when both an opening and a closing marker were present, so a response truncated before its closing fence fell through to a fallback that accepted the raw text --- stray fence marker included --- whenever a \texttt{module} keyword appeared anywhere in it. Verilator then rejected the marker as an undefined preprocessor directive. We hardened the parser to reject an unterminated fence outright. We report the correction here with two honest qualifications. First, the defect is far smaller than we initially assessed: it affects 7 saved submissions campaign-wide (5 Gemini 2.5 Pro, 1 Sonnet, 1 Llama 4 Maverick), not the much larger figure an early count suggested, and only 9 submissions in the whole campaign are truncated at all. Second, and more importantly, the fix is score-neutral by construction: under the old parser a truncated response became an unlintable file scoring zero, and under the new parser it is rejected as unextractable, also scoring zero. Fixing the parser therefore changes no model's score, and none of the improvement in the sensitivity run above is attributable to it --- that improvement comes from the raised token budget alone. We state this explicitly because the opposite inference (that a harness bug was suppressing a model's score, and that repairing it raised the score) is the natural reading and is wrong.

\paragraph{Triaging the 0\% designs, and what the operator mix does and does not license.} A
kill-rate figure is only as meaningful as the faults behind it, so we inspected the individual
surviving mutants of the three 0\% designs rather than resting on the percentage. The results
qualify one of our claims and sharpen another.

For \texttt{square\_wave} (6 mutants) and \texttt{adder\_8bit} (1 mutant) the 0\% is severe and the
small denominators do not soften it, because of \emph{which} faults survive. \texttt{square\_wave}'s
survivors include two \texttt{blocking\_output\_inversion} mutants --- a combinational output
assignment inverted outright --- plus a \texttt{comparator\_boundary\_flip} turning an equality into
an inequality. \texttt{adder\_8bit}'s single mutant is an \texttt{output\_inversion}: its sum output
inverted. A testbench that accepts an inverted primary output is not making a weak measurement, it
is making no measurement of that output at all, and one such survivor establishes that as firmly as
twenty would. We therefore \emph{withdraw} the mitigating framing that \texttt{adder\_8bit}'s
single-mutant denominator makes its result uninformative: the denominator is small, but the fault it
misses is maximally basic.

\texttt{edge\_detect} (10 mutants, 0\%) is the opposite case and we downgrade it accordingly. All
ten of its mutants are the \emph{same} operator, \texttt{assignment\_hold} (a registered assignment
replaced by a hold of its previous value). Ten instances of one fault class is not ten independent
probes, so the correct reading is narrow: this testbench does not detect register-hold faults. It is
not evidence that it misses a broad range of fault types, because no other type was injected.
Five other audited designs are similarly single-operator, and their outcomes span the full range
(\texttt{adder\_bcd} 100\%, \texttt{freq\_div} 100\%, \texttt{ROM} 100\%, \texttt{RAM} 60\%,
\texttt{synchronizer} 50\%), which is itself a caution against over-reading any individual design's figure.

The aggregate operator mix bears on this directly, and we report it rather than leave the reader to
infer it: of 775 generated mutants, 367 (47\%) are \texttt{assignment\_hold}, 154
\texttt{blocking\_output\_inversion}, 92 \texttt{comparator\_boundary\_flip}, 60
\texttt{output\_inversion}, 49 \texttt{bitwise\_inversion}, 29 \texttt{logic\_inversion}, 14
\texttt{shift\_inversion}, 6 \texttt{operator\_inversion}, and 4 \texttt{reset\_polarity\_flip}.
Survival rates differ sharply by operator --- 80\% of
\texttt{bitwise\_inversion} and 69\% of \texttt{logic\_inversion} mutants survive, against 12\% of
\texttt{output\_inversion} and none of the four \texttt{reset\_polarity\_flip} --- so the pooled
figure is partly a function of which operators our generator happens to place most often on this
corpus. This is a real limitation on the precision of cross-design comparison, and it means our
kill rates should be read as sensitivity to \emph{this} operator distribution rather than as a
benchmark-independent quality score. Beyond the specific designs named above, we did not manually
triage the remaining survivors, and we do not claim all 320 aggregate survivors have been
individually confirmed as genuine misses.

\paragraph{Our own suite was gated on the metric it is measured by; RTLLM's was not.} The most
serious objection to this paper's central comparison is that it is not like-for-like. Our 60
testbenches were authored in a project that applies a $\ge$95\% mutation-kill gate, and some were
revised until they cleared it; RTLLM's authors never saw this metric. Comparing our certified rates
against their measured ones therefore risks comparing a tuned quantity to a held-out one --- a
Goodhart problem --- and reporting ``100\% versus 73\% below floor'' without that context would
overstate the result. We quantify the exposure rather than argue about it.

Auditing the full commit history of all 60 testbenches, exactly ten were ever modified in response
to a mutation result, all on one work item (the \texttt{SB-023} chain). For each of those ten we
re-measured the \emph{pre-revision} testbench under the \emph{current} engine, holding the reference
RTL fixed (we verified all ten references are byte-identical between the pre-revision baseline
commit and now, so the mutant sets are the same and the comparison isolates testbench strength
rather than conflating it with later engine improvements). Their pre-revision kill rates were:
\texttt{t2\_uart\_tx} 52.6\%, \texttt{t2\_spi\_master} 63.6\%, \texttt{t2\_uart\_rx} 65.7\%,
\texttt{t3\_sequential\_divider} 74.3\%, \texttt{t2\_delay\_trigger} 75.0\%,
\texttt{t2\_i2c\_slave} 80.0\%, \texttt{t2\_stream\_upsizer} 80.0\%,
\texttt{t2\_stream\_downsizer} 88.2\%, \texttt{t2\_axi\_lite\_regfile} 95.2\%, and
\texttt{t2\_spi\_slave} 95.5\% --- a median of 77.5\%, with eight of the ten below the 95\% floor
at that time. On these ten tasks the Goodhart objection lands directly. But it does not resolve
cleanly the way we originally reported it, because of the generator defect described in
Section~\ref{sec:rigor}: the ``revision'' that was supposed to move these ten testbenches above the
floor turned out to partly consist of the same unsound equivalent-mutant exclusion, not solely
genuine test-vector strengthening. Re-measured honestly today, only three of the ten
(\texttt{t3\_sequential\_divider}, \texttt{t2\_delay\_trigger}, \texttt{t2\_stream\_upsizer})
currently clear 95\%; the other seven are back below it. The Goodhart problem this paragraph set out
to quantify and the generator bug Section~\ref{sec:rigor} discloses are not independent: for these
seven tasks, tuning toward the metric and quietly excluding inconvenient mutants from the metric
were, in practice, the same revision effort.

Two facts bound how far this lands, and both cut against a clean story. First, the equivalent-mutant
bug was not confined to the ten revised tasks: it also reached four tasks that were never revised for
kill-rate reasons at all (\texttt{t2\_priority\_interrupt\_controller},
\texttt{t2\_round\_robin\_arbiter}, \texttt{t2\_pulse\_stretcher}, \texttt{t3\_lru\_tracker}), all
four of which are also below the floor once the bug is removed. A third, independent mechanism
(Section~\ref{sec:rigor}'s later, separate correction to what the kill-rate metric itself counted)
reaches three more tasks that were touched by neither the Goodhart revision nor the equivalent-mutant
bug: \texttt{t2\_running\_min\_max\_tracker}, \texttt{t3\_saturating\_accumulator}, and
\texttt{t2\_pulse\_width\_meter} each had exactly one formal-only kill (two, for the tracker) counted
toward an apparent 100\% under the old blended metric, and fall to 86.7--94.4\% once the rate is
computed from simulation alone. The 14 tasks now below 95\% are therefore the union of three distinct
problems --- a Goodhart effect on the ten revised tasks, an equivalent-mutant-exclusion defect applied
irrespective of revision history, and a metric-definition defect that let formal kills silently
substitute for simulation kills --- not a single clean phenomenon. Of the remaining 50 testbenches that
were never revised for kill-rate reasons, 43 clear the floor as originally authored and untouched by
any of the three mechanisms above; that 43-task subset is the cleanest within-suite comparison
available. Second, the direction of the original Goodhart correction is still informative on the
subset it actually describes: the ten revised testbenches' pre-revision median (77.5\%) sits close
to RTLLM's measured median (74.0\% across all 46 of its audited designs), consistent with revision
being what separates an ungated median from a gated one, on the tasks that were genuinely gated
rather than merely exempted from testing. We report this as a compound finding rather than force it
into the cleaner story we set out to measure.

We flag one residual asymmetry we cannot remove. The 46 genuinely-unaffected testbenches were not
iterated against their kill rates, but most were authored in a project that already had a
$\ge$95\% gate, so their authors wrote to that standard even without measuring against it. That is
genuinely weaker
than RTLLM's blindness to the metric and genuinely stronger than iterating until a task passes; we
name the distinction rather than claim the 46 are a true held-out control. A fully blind comparison
would require testbenches authored before the gate existed, which for most of this suite no longer
exists in the history.

\paragraph{Six tasks were passed by no model, and we have not audited them.} Our own audit logic --- that a testbench nothing ever fails is a testbench worth interrogating --- has a mirror image we should apply to ourselves: a task that every model fails is a candidate for being broken, misspecified, or accidentally unsatisfiable, not necessarily a hard task. Six of the 60 Track~A tasks were passed by none of the seven models at the reported condition: \texttt{t1\_mod\_n\_counter}, \texttt{t2\_majority\_filter}, \texttt{t2\_pulse\_stretcher}, \texttt{t2\_round\_robin\_arbiter}, \texttt{t2\_stream\_upsizer}, and \texttt{t2\_uart\_rx}. (At the lower output cap the zero-pass set was both larger and different --- ten tasks --- which is itself evidence that a zero-pass result can reflect the experimental condition rather than the task.) Each has a maintainer-signed-off reference implementation that passes the full pipeline by construction, so none is unsatisfiable in the strict sense --- but that establishes only that \emph{a} solution exists, not that the specification communicates it adequately or that the hidden vectors are not over-constrained relative to the prose. We have not performed a per-task solvability review of these six, and we name them explicitly so that a reader can weight them appropriately rather than discovering the zero-pass set by recomputation.

\paragraph{Tier difficulty is confounded by extraction failures.} Raw per-tier pass rates at the reported condition are Tier~1 73.6\%, Tier~2 41.7\%, and Tier~3 56.2\% --- a non-monotonicity in which Tier~2 appears harder than Tier~3. Part of this is an artifact of the no-extraction failures discussed above, which concentrate on the longer Tier-2 and Tier-3 specifications. Excluding pairs where no submission was produced at all, the rates become Tier~1 74.6\%, Tier~2 44.2\%, and Tier~3 59.0\%. The non-monotonicity narrows but does not disappear, so we report it as a real if smaller effect --- plausibly because Tier~2's protocol and handshake tasks demand exact multi-cycle interface conformance, which our hidden vectors check strictly, whereas several Tier-3 datapaths are arithmetically intricate but interface-simple.

\paragraph{Applying the same denominator scrutiny to our own suite.} The mutant-count caveat raised above for RTLLM's audited designs (Section~\ref{sec:audit-results}) applies with the same force to our own 60 Track A testbenches: their mutant counts (counting only the valid, non-stillborn denominator, Section~\ref{sec:rigor}) range from 3 to 263 with a median of 11, and 22 of the 60 have fewer than 10 mutants, meaning a single survivor in those tasks necessarily fails the 95\% floor while a task with 30+ mutants can retain several survivors and still pass. We hold RTLLM to a standard our own suite shares, not a stricter one, and disclose it symmetrically rather than only where it favors our own certification claims. Only 46 of those 60 currently clear that floor at all (Section~\ref{sec:rigor}); this denominator caveat applies to the 46 that do, not as a separate concern from the 14 that do not. Separately, Track B's 8 testbenches are not yet certified under the mutation-audit protocol described in Section~\ref{sec:rigor}; only the Track A testbenches carry that certification as of this writing (and, as of this writing, only 46 of the 60 carry it successfully), and extending certification to Track B, and strengthening the 14 below-floor Track A testbenches to genuinely clear it, are both future work. The area-reduction Track B objective's lack of \texttt{sec} coverage (Section~\ref{sec:trackb}) is a related, disclosed gap in the same direction. Finally, the human-review sign-off described in Section~\ref{sec:suite} is performed by this paper's sole author; it substitutes single-maintainer scrutiny for the multi-reviewer process a larger project would use, and we do not claim the independence multiple reviewers would provide.

\paragraph{Four Track B protocol gaps we found only after the reported campaign, not before it.} All four are disclosed here with the same precision this paper applies to its own generator and parser defects (Section~\ref{sec:rigor}, Section~\ref{sec:limitations} above), because Table~\ref{tab:trackb}'s campaign ran under the code that had them, not the code that has since fixed them.

First, \texttt{read\_file}'s claimed boundary (Section~\ref{sec:trackb}) was not enforced for this campaign: the tool had no allowlist at all, only a check that a path could not escape the sandbox entirely, so it could in principle reach any file the sandbox contained. Auditing all 56 retained official transcripts, we found five actions across two models that successfully read a task's public testbench: Sonnet read \texttt{b3}'s (reduce-area FIR) testbench twice and \texttt{b7}'s (arbiter fairness) once; GPT-5 read \texttt{b2}'s (multiplier timing closure) and \texttt{b8}'s (AXI byte-enable) once each. None of these reads reached the hidden scoring vectors, which are merged into the testbench only at scoring time and are never copied into the agent's sandbox at all, so no agent gained access to the actual pass/fail criteria. We name the more pointed fact rather than let a reader compute it themselves: \texttt{b7} and \texttt{b8} are, respectively, one of Sonnet's three Track B successes and GPT-5's \emph{only} Track B success (Section~\ref{sec:trackb}), while \texttt{b3} and \texttt{b2} --- the other two read tasks --- were both misses for the model that read them. We have no evidence this reading caused either success --- a public smoke testbench is a weaker signal than the hidden vectors that actually decide pass/fail, and both models' successes on other, never-read tasks show the tool is not necessary for winning --- but we cannot rule it out either, and a reviewer should not have to take our word for a boundary the tool did not actually enforce. We have since added a strict allowlist restricting \texttt{read\_file} to the design directory only (Section~\ref{sec:trackb}), confirmed directly against this exact scenario (repeating the census's own action against a live sandbox under the fixed tool now returns a rejection instead of the testbench content), but the campaign Table~\ref{tab:trackb} reports predates that fix and we do not re-run it here; a re-run under the corrected tool, or an explicit accounting of which reported results the exposure could plausibly have touched, is future work rather than something this paper resolves.

Second, and a direct companion to the first gap, the protocol gave an agent no way to discover what was actually there to read: the first prompt sent to an agent contained only the task ID and an empty transcript, and the action protocol offered exact-path \texttt{read\_file} but no directory listing or file inventory of any kind, so an agent had to guess a path was correct before learning whether it existed at all. A direct census of every \texttt{read\_file} action across the 56 retained official transcripts found 110 attempts, of which only 30 succeeded; 38 of the 56 runs never had a single successful read, and 21 never attempted one. The reads that did succeed depended on guessing conventional names such as \texttt{spec.md} or a task's known design path, while many failed attempts guessed plausible-sounding files this protocol's actual layout never used, such as \texttt{README.md}, \texttt{design.sv}, or \texttt{task.md}. Section~\ref{sec:trackb}'s description of an agent ``provisioned with a checked-out repository'' is accurate about what the sandbox contained but overstates what the protocol let an agent find out was there; nothing in the protocol resembled directory listing until the fix described next. We have since added exactly the two remedies this gap calls for: the first prompt now discloses \texttt{design\_files}, the real sorted listing of the design directory, at zero \texttt{tool\_calls} cost, and a new \texttt{list\_files} action lets an agent re-list on demand through the same JSON protocol as every other tool, both backed by one shared helper so the two can never disagree (Section~\ref{sec:trackb}). As with the boundary gap above, the fix postdates the reported campaign, so the 38-of-56 runs with zero successful reads in Table~\ref{tab:trackb} should be read as reflecting this discoverability gap at least as much as any genuine decision by the agent that reading supporting files was unnecessary.

Third, the per-task token budget (Section~\ref{sec:trackb}) was measurably not enforced as strictly as ``strict... budget'' there implies. The loop that checks tokens against budget handed the entire remaining balance to the next provider call as pure output allowance, reserving nothing for that call's own input tokens, and a call whose action happened to be \texttt{done} was allowed to complete before the post-call budget check ran rather than after. Auditing all 56 official manifests against their declared \texttt{objective.yaml} budgets, 31 exceeded their nominal token budget, by as much as 24{,}652 tokens in one case; one of those 31 --- GPT-5's \texttt{b8\_axi\_byte\_enables} run, the same task discussed above --- recorded \texttt{budget\_exceeded: null} despite finishing at 155{,}657 tokens against a 150{,}000-token budget (5{,}657 over), because the run's final call was a \texttt{done} that the old check-ordering never re-evaluated against the budget it had just exceeded. We have fixed both defects: a conservative input-token reservation before each call, and an unconditional budget re-check after every call including one ending in \texttt{done}. As with the read-boundary gap above, the fix postdates the reported campaign. The cost figures in Table~\ref{tab:trackb} are the actual metered costs of the runs as they happened, so they are not inflated by this bug, but the \emph{budget-exceeded} classification recorded for those 31 runs, and specifically the false negative on \texttt{b8}, should be read as unreliable rather than authoritative.

Fourth, and most seriously, none of the 56 official Track B manifests underlying Table~\ref{tab:trackb} retained the design source they scored: each was written to a temporary sandbox directory (recorded literally, e.g.\ \texttt{/tmp/siliconbench-agentb-r79ylx19/submission}) that was deleted before the run finished, and the manifest schema at the time recorded neither a content hash nor a copy of the submitted RTL, so \texttt{submission\_sha256} is absent from every one of the 56. This directly contradicts the reproducibility claim stated earlier in this section (``given the pinned image digest, the submission file, \ldots{} reproducing any published score depends on no other input''): the second of those three required inputs does not exist for any Track B result this paper reports, so no reviewer, and not even we ourselves, can independently re-score any Table~\ref{tab:trackb} entry against the exact RTL an agent submitted. The fix has two parts, one closed and one open. Closed: submission content is now hashed and a design sidecar is written alongside every new manifest, and we added an enforcement check that a future official manifest committed without a reproducible design fails the test suite outright, so this exact failure mode cannot recur silently. Open, and not resolved by this paper: the 56 historical manifests remain permanently unreproducible, because the bytes they scored are gone, not merely unhashed; recovering them would require re-running the campaign under spend approval we have not sought, and we report the gap rather than paper over it with a partial reconstruction. Table~\ref{tab:trackb}'s figures are exactly what the harness recorded at scoring time and we have no reason to doubt them, but ``no reason to doubt'' and ``independently reproducible'' are different claims, and only the pinned-digest paragraph's Track A instance of this section currently supports the stronger one.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

The prevailing paradigm for evaluating large language models on register-transfer-level (RTL) design predominantly assesses the functional correctness of generated code. VerilogEval~\cite{liu2023verilogeval} established this framework utilizing a suite of tasks derived from the HDLBits teaching platform, evaluated via simulation testbenches under a pass@k protocol; its subsequent iteration~\cite{pinckney2024revisiting} expanded to specification-to-RTL generation, introduced in-context prompting, and implemented granular failure classification. RTLLM~\cite{lu2024rtllm} adopted a complementary approach, originally curating thirty designs encompassing arithmetic and logic circuits, each formalized as a triplet comprising a natural-language specification, a testbench, and a human-authored reference; the project's public repository has since expanded to fifty designs under the same MIT license, released by the authors as RTLLM v2.0~\cite{liu2025openllmrtl}, and is the primary target of the external audit reported in Section~\ref{sec:audit-results}. RTLLM's own evaluation flow synthesizes generated RTL and reports post-synthesis PPA (worst-negative-slack, area, and power) against its reference designs, so it is not a correctness-only benchmark; what it does not report is a mutation-kill or equivalent systematic fault-coverage measurement of its own testbenches' rigor, which is exactly the property Table~\ref{tab:related} and Section~\ref{sec:audit-results} address. Notably, RTLLM's own authors have separately identified benchmark-quality erosion as a problem worth solving: RTL-BenchMT~\cite{wang2026rtlbenchmt}, from the same group, proposes an agentic framework that dynamically detects flawed benchmark cases and revises them to guard against overfitting. This is a genuinely different mechanism from ours --- ongoing, first-party revision of a benchmark's own cases, rather than a one-shot, third-party mutation audit of testbench sensitivity on a fixed snapshot --- but it is independent evidence, from inside the benchmark's own maintaining lab, that the concern this paper raises about testbench and task quality is one the field is starting to treat as a first-class problem rather than something we are alone in flagging. These foundational benchmarks codified a critical distinction: syntactic validity diverges significantly from functional correctness. Our own campaign illustrates the same gap concretely: even our highest-scoring model, GPT-5, passes only 43 of 60 (72\%) Track A tasks (Section~\ref{sec:results}), and Section~\ref{sec:limitations} reports that 78.6\% of failing submissions that produced any code at all fail before ever reaching simulation, at Stage~0 lint. Neither VerilogEval nor RTLLM reports a mutation-kill floor for its own testbenches --- the gap this paper's audit methodology is designed to measure. Mutation testing itself predates this literature by decades, originating in software engineering with DeMillo, Lipton, and Sayward's foundational proposal to inject faults into a program and measure what fraction a test suite detects~\cite{demillo1978hints}. Prior work has already carried that idea into hardware verification, outside the LLM-benchmark literature: Huang~et~al.~\cite{huang2015mutation} apply mutation analysis to qualify hardware testbench quality, Mantra~\cite{wu2023mantra} derives RTL mutation operators from real reported bugs, and AutoBench~\cite{qiu2024autobench} proposes automated HDL testbench generation and evaluation. Closer to our own tooling, MCY~\cite{yosyshq2021mcy} is a general-purpose, actively maintained mutation-coverage tool built on the same Yosys toolchain our own PPA flow uses (Section~\ref{sec:related}): given a design and a self-checking testbench, it generates post-synthesis netlist mutations, uses formal equivalence checking to discard mutants provably identical to the original before scoring, and reports testbench coverage over the survivors. That formal-filtering step is a more principled solution to a problem this paper's own methodology section (Section~\ref{sec:rigor}) reports hitting directly: our reference suite's mutant generator once excluded mutants via hand-authored equivalence reasoning in source comments, and when we tested that reasoning against the real hidden testbench, half of the excluded mutants turned out not to be equivalent at all. MCY targets arbitrary Yosys-synthesizable designs generally, not existing public LLM RTL-generation benchmarks' own shipped testbenches specifically; applying MCY-style formal mutant-equivalence filtering to our own or an audited benchmark's mutant set, rather than the simulation-only kill rate both currently report, is future work this comparison makes concrete rather than a difference we currently claim credit for closing. None of these four --- Huang~et~al., Mantra, AutoBench, or MCY --- targets an existing public LLM RTL-generation benchmark's own shipped testbenches, which is this paper's narrower and more specific contribution.

Table~\ref{tab:related} summarizes recent RTL-generation and system-level LLM benchmarks against
two properties central to this paper: whether the benchmark reports a mutation-testing (or
equivalent systematic fault-injection) rigor measurement of its own testbenches, and whether it
scores generated designs on post-synthesis PPA rather than functional correctness alone. ChipBench~\cite{yu2026chipbench}
evaluates Verilog generation, debugging, and reference-model synthesis across three task families
using directed and constrained-random testing; ArchXBench~\cite{purini2025archxbench} scales
generation difficulty across six complexity tiers from logic primitives to full accelerators;
SLDB~\cite{alvanaki2025sldb} evaluates system-level integration and configuration of accelerators
into heterogeneous SoCs rather than module-level generation; and ProtocolLLM~\cite{sheth2025protocolllm}
narrows scope to SystemVerilog generation for four communication protocols (SPI, I\textsuperscript{2}C,
UART, AXI), evaluating syntax, synthesizability, and timing fidelity. Three more recent entries
emerged since our own reference suite was frozen: ChipVerilog~\cite{tan2026chipverilog} targets
larger, hierarchical OpenCores-derived designs (up to 1{,}000+ lines across five design families)
that expose cross-module integration failures single-module benchmarks cannot; RTL-BenchLS~\cite{wang2026rtlbenchls}
scales to over 10{,}000 formally verified designs and adds three reasoning-style evaluation tasks
beyond specification-to-RTL generation; and RTL-BenchMT~\cite{wang2026rtlbenchmt}, discussed above,
targets benchmark maintenance rather than model evaluation directly. None of these seven reports a
mutation-testing or systematic fault-coverage measurement of its own testbenches in its published
paper or public repository, and none reports post-synthesis PPA scoring of the RTL it evaluates ---
based on the papers, repositories, and documentation we were able to access; we did not exhaustively
audit every appendix or supplementary artifact, and report this as the most accurate characterization
available rather than a certified negative claim.

We should be explicit about what Table~\ref{tab:related} is and is not. Its two columns are the two
properties this paper contributes, so the table is a positioning aid, not a general capability
comparison, and it would be misleading to read it as a scorecard on which GateTruth simply wins.
Several of the listed benchmarks lead decisively on dimensions the table does not show: CVDP spans
783 problems across 13 task categories against our 68, an order of magnitude more task diversity;
VerilogEval's second iteration contributes the granular failure classification our own campaign only
acquired late (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}); and every benchmark listed has been exercised by more
independent parties than ours, which has been run by its sole author. Dimensions on which we would
expect to compare unfavorably --- problem count, multi-simulator support, multi-sample pass@$k$
estimation, and independent replication --- are precisely the ones omitted, and we name them here
rather than let a two-column table imply they do not exist.

\label{tab:related}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lp{4.7cm}cc}
\toprule
Benchmark & Scope & Mutation rigor & PPA \\
\midrule

NVIDIA's CVDP~\cite{pinckney2025cvdp} takes a substantially broader approach, spanning code generation, code comprehension, and both agentic and non-agentic evaluation across 783 problems in 13 task categories, with an Apache-2.0 harness and a public dataset whose non-code content is CC~BY~4.0 and whose code is Apache-2.0. CVDP is also the foundation of the Si2 (Silicon Integration Initiative) LLM Benchmarking Coalition, an industry effort co-chaired by NVIDIA's Nathaniel Pinckney and Synopsys's Ramesh Narayanaswamy, which extends CVDP with additional problem categories and operates a public results leaderboard (LBC-bench, launched 2026). As detailed in Section~\ref{sec:audit-method}, CVDP's public release deliberately withholds reference solutions to mitigate evaluation contamination; this is a sound design choice for CVDP's own scoring purpose but leaves the benchmark's own testbench rigor unauditable via mutation testing from the public release alone, a limitation we report rather than route around.

Research engaging with post-synthesis metrics has predominantly approached the problem from predictive modeling rather than generation scoring. MetRex~\cite{abdelatty2025metrex} compiled a comprehensive dataset of Verilog designs correlated with post-synthesis area, delay, and static power to evaluate whether models can infer these metrics from source code, while related frameworks like RocketPPA~\cite{abdollahi2025rocketppa} train models for code-level PPA prediction. Although these works advance metric estimation, they do not evaluate the physical viability of generated designs executed through an actual synthesis flow, nor do they address testbench rigor. GateTruth's own reference suite enforces a rigidly deterministic pipeline --- a single pinned container image identified by a maintainer-set build marker rather than a content hash (Section~\ref{sec:rigor}), uniform liberty and clock targets per task, a fixed Yosys-plus-OpenSTA path, and SHA-256 integrity checksums over canonical-JSON results --- so that PPA comparisons produced by it are reproducible directly from the recorded submission and pinned image.

In summary, GateTruth is, to our knowledge, the first tool to apply mutation-testing certification to existing public RTL-generation benchmarks and report the result, and the first to combine that audit methodology with a mutation-certified reference implementation, permissively licensed and intended for open publication (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}), used to validate it before external application (self-certified under a published protocol by this paper's sole author, not independently reviewed; Section~\ref{sec:limitations}). It uniquely combines: (a) a deterministic, seeded mutation-audit protocol applicable to any RTL benchmark with a golden reference and a runnable testbench; (b) an explicit, non-silent policy for benchmarks or designs that cannot be audited (\texttt{unsupported} status, or a documented structural finding, rather than a misleading score); (c) a 68-task, dual-track reference suite, intended for open publication, in which the same protocol is applied to every one of the suite's 60 Track A testbenches before external use, certifying 46 of them and reporting the remaining 14 as a genuine finding rather than omitting them; (d) an RTL-to-PPA synthesis-and-timing flow whose manifest schema enforces determinism as a contract and which we have spot-checked, not proven exhaustively per task (Section~\ref{sec:rigor}), underlying that reference suite's independent, secondary contribution as a model/agent benchmark; and (e) a temporal sensitivity rerun showing that the per-call output-token budget --- a parameter most RTL benchmarks neither vary nor report --- coincided with a leaderboard reordering, which we surfaced by applying the same scepticism to our own instrument that the audit applies to others', while disclosing the confounds (Section~\ref{sec:limitations}) that keep this from being a controlled, single-variable result.

\appendix

\section{Run-to-Run Variance}
\label{app:variance}

The v1.0 leaderboard reports a single run per model. Because model generation is not
deterministic (and the reasoning models do not accept a fixed temperature), we quantify
run-to-run spread by re-running the three Anthropic models over all 60 Track A tasks three
times each, at the identical 16{,}384-token, pinned-image condition Table~\ref{tab:tracka}
itself reports: the already-committed single run stands as one of the three, and we ran two
further official re-runs (2026-08-03, \$5.63) for exactly this purpose. Table~\ref{tab:variance}
is a robustness measurement alongside the single-run leaderboard, not a replacement for it. One
scope limit applies: these runs cover only the three Anthropic models, so the four non-Anthropic
models --- including Gemini 2.5 Pro, whose score is the most condition-sensitive in the campaign
(Section~\ref{sec:limitations}) --- carry no variance estimate at all, and the comparisons in
Section~\ref{sec:results} that involve them are correspondingly weaker. An earlier pilot of this
study (2026-07-26, \$8.18) was run at the since-superseded 4096-token condition and measured a
substantially larger spread ($\sigma \approx 4$); because it characterizes a condition this paper
no longer reports as its leaderboard, we do not reproduce its table here, and every $\sigma$ cited
elsewhere in this paper now refers to the measurement below, not that pilot.

Every figure in Table~\ref{tab:variance} is generated by
\texttt{paper/data/generate\_variance\_appendix.py} from nine signed, committed per-run manifests
--- three per model, all at the identical 16{,}384-token, pinned-image condition --- the same
reproducibility bar every other table in this paper meets (Section~\ref{sec:rigor}). An earlier
draft of this appendix could not make that claim: its nine per-run manifests were not committed
alongside a generator, and its figures were reported as recorded at run time rather than
independently re-derivable from evidence a reader can check today. That gap is now closed.

\centering
\caption{Track A run-to-run variance over three runs per model at the reported 16{,}384-token
condition (GateTruth Score, 0--100). Standard deviation is the sample standard deviation
(Bessel-corrected, $n-1$ denominator). ``Single run'' is the same figure Table~\ref{tab:tracka}
reports and is one of the three runs the mean is computed over, not a fourth, independent point.}
\label{tab:variance}

Two observations follow, both real but more modest than the superseded 4096-token pilot's numbers
suggested. First, run-to-run standard deviation at the reported condition is genuine for the
frontier models --- 1.85 points for Opus, 2.53 for Sonnet --- and smaller still for Haiku (0.73);
with only $n=3$ per model these remain imprecise estimates, and we report them as a directional
signal rather than a tight interval, but they are now committed, checkable measurements at the
condition this paper actually leaderboards, not a carried-over guess from a different cap. Second,
Opus and Sonnet remain not decisively separated on Track A ($46.18 \pm 1.85$ vs $45.01 \pm
2.53$: heavily overlapping ranges, a mean gap of 1.17 against either model's own standard
deviation; this is a descriptive read of overlapping intervals at $n=3$, not a formal equivalence
test with a preregistered margin), though the direction differs from the superseded pilot: there, Sonnet's three-run mean
edged above Opus's; here, Opus leads on both the single reported run (46.99 vs 42.09) and the
three-run mean (46.18 vs 45.01). We read this as a real but not decisive lead, well inside the
overlap of the two ranges, not as a reversal of the underlying no-decisive-separation finding, and
the sign-flip between the two studies is itself a demonstration of exactly the run-to-run noise
this appendix exists to quantify. The models' reliable separation appears in the agentic-repair
track (Section~\ref{sec:trackb}), not in static generation. We therefore recommend that future
versions report mean $\pm$ standard deviation over at least three runs as the default leaderboard
cell, and publish the individual per-run scores alongside the summary statistics so readers are not
dependent on our aggregation choices.
